Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources I've gathered. Here is the commentary:

---

## 2 Samuel 12 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Then the LORD sent Nathan to David…"

- **The timing:** Between chapters 11 and 12 there was a gap of about 9–12 months (the child had been born by v. 14). During this time David remained unrepentant and his sin festered. Psalm 32:3–4 describes this period: David's "body wasted away," his "vitality was drained." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-12-commentary)
- **God took the initiative**: The LORD is mentioned in 2 Samuel 11 only in the very last verse, but here God actively intervenes. Nathan didn't volunteer — he was *sent*. "The truth is that sinners never seek God, until He seeks us." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_samuel_121-14_commentary)
- **Grace in sending a prophet**: Matthew Henry observed that one would think God should have sent enemies or terrors — instead, "He sent a prophet to him." God mercifully kept speaking to David even when David didn't listen. Yet we should not presume God will strive with the unrepentant forever (Gen 6:3). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Nathan's courage**: Nathan had to confront a king with absolute power of life and death over sins of adultery and murder. J. Vernon McGee called Nathan "the bravest man in the Bible." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_samuel_12-commentary)
- **Nathan's credibility**: He was already known to David — the same prophet who had delivered the glorious Davidic Covenant promise in 2 Samuel 7. This made David more receptive. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- Ellicott notes that Nathan was "already on intimate terms with David, and recognised by him as a prophet." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### vv. 1–4 — The Parable of the Rich Man and the Poor Man's Lamb

- **Purpose of the parable**: Nathan wisely constructed it "by not having too near a resemblance, to make David unwittingly pass sentence on himself." The parable was to David "what his own letter was in the hands of the brave Uriah" (2 Sam 11:14). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_samuel_121-14_commentary)
- Ellicott: "The parable is designed to bring out David's indignation against the offender without being so clear as to awaken at first any suspicion of a personal application. It does not allude to the special crimes of David, but to the meanness and selfishness of the transaction." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **The sin as theft**: David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that the parable frames David's sin as *theft* — stealing from Uriah what belonged to him in marriage (citing 1 Cor 7:3–5). "Adultery and sexual immorality are sins in many ways, and in one aspect are theft – taking something that does not belong to us." The same principle applies to pornography and lust. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **John Piper (Desiring God)** makes a strong point: Nathan's parable portrays Bathsheba as the helpless little ewe lamb — taken, killed, and consumed. Piper argues the parable shows David didn't merely commit adultery but used his power to *force* Bathsheba, such that "we are not exaggerating to use the word rape for David's abuse of his power." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/did-bathsheba-sin-with-david)
- **The tender description** (v. 3): The lamb ate from the poor man's food, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, "was like a daughter to him." Ellicott: "All these circumstances are exquisitely contrived to heighten the pity of the hearer for the oppressed, and his indignation against the oppressor." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### vv. 5–6 — David's Outraged Judgment

- **David's anger**: "David's generous impulses had not been extinguished by his sin, nor his warm sense of justice; his naturally quick temper at once roused his indignation to the utmost." (Ellicott) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **Self-deception**: David showed that we often try to rid our guilty consciences by passing harsh judgment on someone else. Guzik: "David had to condemn his own sin before he could find forgiveness. We often try to find refuge in excusing or minimizing or deflecting the blame for our sin." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Death sentence**: David commanded death, though it wasn't a capital crime under the Law. The oath "As the LORD lives" reveals his passionate indignation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Fourfold restitution**: David cited Exodus 22:1 — the exact Mosaic penalty for stealing a sheep. Guzik: "David's sin and hardness of heart did not diminish his knowledge of the Bible. He knew the words of the Bible but was distant from the Author." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
  - The Berean Study Bible notes a grim irony: David lost *four sons* — the child born to Bathsheba, Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah — fulfilling the fourfold restitution he had pronounced. (https://biblehub.com/study/2_samuel/12.htm)
  - The LXX reads "sevenfold" and the Chaldee reads "fortyfold" — expressing more human indignation — but David knew the Law too well to change its terms. (Ellicott) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### v. 7 — "You are the man!"

- **The shock**: Nathan applied the parable with alarming simplicity and boldness. Trapp: "This was downright plain dealing indeed." Ellicott says the shock aroused David's "slumbering conscience." This could not have happened had David been "essentially a bad man." His conscience had been "stupefied by the delirium of prosperity and power." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **Personal conviction needed**: Maclaren (quoted in Guzik): "God accuses us and condemns us one by one that He may save us one by one." It wasn't enough for David to confess he was a sinner in general — he had to confess *this* sin at *this* point. "You cannot frighten men into repentance, you may frighten them into remorse." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### vv. 7–9 — God's Indictment: Ingratitude and Despising the Command

- **Reminder of grace**: Through Nathan, God recalled all He had done for David — anointed him, delivered him from Saul, gave him Saul's house and wives, gave him Israel and Judah — "and if that had been too little, I also would have given you much more." David's sin was fundamentally an expression of *base ingratitude*. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"Thy master's wives"** (v. 8): Ellicott notes this refers to the Oriental custom that the new king had a right to the harem of his predecessor. Only one wife of Saul is recorded (1 Sam 14:50) and one concubine (2 Sam 3:7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **"Despised the commandment of the LORD"** (v. 9): John Piper observes that Nathan's charge was not "Why have you killed a man and raped a woman?" but "Why have you despised the word of God?" The ultimate nature of sin is *vertical* — it is despising God Himself. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/how-could-david-say-to-god-after-sleeping-with-uriahs-wife-and-then-killing-him-against-you-and-you-only-have-i-sinned)
- **"Slain him with the sword"**: Ellicott points out the Hebrew here is a different, stronger word than "killed" earlier — "might well be translated *murdered*." It was murder in God's eyes, though accomplished indirectly by the sword of the Ammonites. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### v. 10 — "The sword will never depart from your house"

- **Because you have despised Me**: In v. 9 God said David despised the *commandment*; here He says David despised *Him*. "We can't despise God's commandments without despising Him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"Never depart"**: Ellicott says "never" here means "as long as David lives." The punishment was realized in a long succession of woes — from Amnon's murder to Adonijah's execution. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **God still calls Bathsheba "the wife of Uriah the Hittite"**: God "didn't even use Bathsheba's own name. He wanted David to consider Bathsheba not only as an individual but also as the wife of Uriah the Hittite." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### vv. 11–12 — Adversity from David's Own House; Public Shame

- **"I will raise up adversity against you from your own house"**: The Living Bible translates "adversity" as "rebellion." Because David troubled another man's house, God would allow trouble to arise from within David's own house. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor"**: As David violated another's wife, so another would violate his wives. This was fulfilled in 2 Samuel 16:21–22 when Absalom lay with David's concubines on the rooftop. Trapp notes it may have been "on that same terrace from whence he first looked, liked, and lusted after Bath-sheba." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"You did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, before the sun"**: Gill notes God would "suffer it to be done, and so order it in his providence" — David's leaving his wives behind, Ahithophel's wicked counsel, Absalom's lust, and no one in Israel having the courage to protest. The phrase "under the sun" implies this scandal would be known wherever the sun shines, which has been fulfilled through Scripture. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_samuel_121-14_commentary)

### v. 13a — David's Confession: "I have sinned against the LORD"

- **Just two Hebrew words**: *hata al-Yahweh*. Guzik: "These two words, and the heart they reflect, show the fundamental difference between David and Saul. Confession doesn't need to be long to be real and sincere." Trapp: "The greatest griefs are not always the most verbal. Saul confessed his sin more largely, but less effectually." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Contrast with Saul**: Ellicott notes that Saul used the same words (1 Sam 15:24, 30) but "in a totally different spirit. Saul's confession was a concession to the prophet for the purpose of securing his support, and with no real penitence; David, in these few words, pours out before God the confession of a broken heart." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **No excuses**: Keil and Delitzsch: "There is no excuse, no hiding, no concealment of the sin. There is no searching for a loophole, no pretext put forward, no human weakness pleaded." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"Against the LORD"**: David's sin against Bathsheba, Uriah, Ahithophel, his family, and the nation were enormous — but his sin against the LORD was greatest of all. G. Campbell Morgan: "In all this David was pre-eminently revealed as a man after God's own heart. Other men who had been guilty of such failure might have defended their actions, might have slain the prophet. Not so with this man." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- Psalm 51 is the fuller, more eloquent expression of this repentance, composed after this encounter. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### vv. 13b–14 — Forgiveness and Consequences

- **Immediate forgiveness**: "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die." God's forgiveness was immediate — no probation period. "You shall not die" meant David would be spared the death penalty for adultery (Lev 20:10) and murder (Lev 24:17) under the Mosaic Law. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Yet consequences remain**: John Piper distinguishes between the consequences of *forgiven* sin (which are "disciplinary consequences") and consequences of *unforgiven* sin (which are proper "penalties"). The aims of consequences for forgiven sin are: (1) to demonstrate the exceeding evil of sin, (2) to show that God does not take sin lightly even when He lays aside punishment, (3) to humble and sanctify the forgiven sinner. "We must not equate forgiveness with absence of painful impact." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-consequences-of-forgiven-sin)
- **"Given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme"**: David did what the enemies of God would do. Trapp: "Hitherto all the king's care had been to conceal his sin from the world, which yet he could not do with all his skill, for the enemies had got it by the end." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- Ellicott: "Although David was forgiven, yet since his sin had brought great scandal on the church, it was necessary that he should suffer publicly the consequences of that sin." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **"The child also who is born to you shall surely die"**: Guzik notes there is a difference between "judgment *for* sin" and "judgment *by* sin." God forgave David's sin but would not shield him from every consequence. Spurgeon: "Long before his sin with Bathsheba, there were various indications as to David's special liability to temptation. That sin only threw out upon the surface the evil that was always within him; and now God, having him see that the deadly cancer is there, begins to use the knife to cut it out of him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Clarke's note**: Clarke argues that the phrase "The LORD hath put away thy sin" means God transferred the *temporal* death penalty to the child rather than David — "He shall die, thou shalt not die." He sees this as distinct from eternal pardon, which David only later sought in Psalm 51. However, this is a minority view; most commentators see full forgiveness being granted at this moment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-samuel-12.html)

### v. 15 — The LORD Struck the Child

- "The biblical writer does not hesitate to attribute directly to the Lord the sickness of this child." (Baldwin, quoted in Guzik) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"Uriah's wife"**: Even though Uriah was dead and David was legally married to Bathsheba, the text still calls her "Uriah's wife" because when the child was conceived, that is who she was. "It is God's way of saying, 'Uriah's death and the subsequent marriage doesn't make everything alright.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Innocent suffering**: Guzik acknowledges this is hard to accept — the innocent often suffers because of the guilty. Yet this was more tragic for David and Bathsheba than for the child himself, who went to eternal glory. "God's mercy to his erring and repentant children will be shown in converting the results of their sin into the fires of their purification" (Meyer). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **A price must be paid**: Even when sin is forgiven, a price is paid. Often an innocent party pays that price — this illustrates the principle that points toward Christ's atoning sacrifice. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### vv. 16–17 — David's Fasting and Prayer

- Ellicott, citing O. von Gerlach: David's prayer "must have sprung from some other source than excessive love of any created object. His great desire was to avert the stroke as a sign of the wrath of God, in the hope that he might be able to discern, in the preservation of the child, a proof of Divine favour consequent upon the restoration of his fellowship with God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- Guzik: David was right to "take the announcement of God's judgment as an invitation to earnestly seek His mercy." We shouldn't receive announced judgment passively or fatalistically. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- The elders of his house tried to raise him, but he refused — a picture of deep, desperate intercession.

### vv. 18–19 — The Child Dies; The Servants' Fear

- **The seventh day**: The child died after seven days of illness. The servants were afraid to tell David, reasoning that if he wouldn't listen to them while the child was alive, how much worse might he react upon hearing of its death. They feared he might "do some harm" (literally, "do evil" or harm himself). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- David perceived the death from the servants' whispering and asked directly. Gill notes that "putting the question to them so closely, they could not avoid giving the answer they did." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-12.html)

### vv. 20–23 — David's Surprising Response

- **Worship after death**: David arose, washed, anointed himself, changed clothes, went to the house of the LORD and *worshiped*, then ate. This shows that "extraordinary prayer and fasting are not tools to get whatever we want from God. They are demonstrations of radical submission and surrender to God's power and will." David's prayer and fasting *were* answered — he had peace knowing he had done all he could to seek mercy. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **"I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me"** (v. 23): Ellicott says these words in David's mouth "can scarcely be anything else than an expression of confidence in a life of consciousness beyond the grave, and of the future recognition of those loved on earth." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- Gill: "from whence it appears, that the Old Testament saints did not suppose an annihilation at death; but believed the immortality of the soul, a future state after death of eternal life and bliss." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-12.html)
- Guzik: "David was confident that his son would meet him in heaven. This is an indication that babies and perhaps children who pass from this world to the next will go to heaven." He adds 1 Cor 7:14 as additional assurance for children of believers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### v. 24 — Solomon Born; David Comforts Bathsheba

- **First time she is called "Bathsheba his wife"**: Before this, the writer consistently called her "the wife of Uriah" (except for the bare mention of her name in 11:3). "Only now, after the chastisement for sin, is she called Bathsheba his wife." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **David did not forsake Bathsheba**: Though the marriage began in sin, David was to honor God in the marriage commitment he had made. Guzik compares this to Paul's principle in 1 Cor 7:17: remain in the calling to which you were called. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- **Solomon** means "peaceable." Gill: "the birth of this son was a confirmation of the peace and reconciliation between God and them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-12.html)
- Ellicott notes that Solomon's birth "could hardly have taken place until after the events mentioned in 2 Samuel 12:26-31," since the siege of Rabbah would not have lasted two years. It is placed here "after the custom of Scripture narrative to close the story of Bath-sheba in its proper connection." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### v. 25 — Jedidiah: "Beloved of the LORD"

- **Nathan names him Jedidiah** ("beloved of the LORD"): This was a special name given by God through Nathan as an expression of divine acceptance. It never came into common use as a personal title. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- Guzik: "God's mercy extends beyond the judgment: Solomon… becomes David's heir and ancestor of the Messiah, demonstrating that God genuinely forgives repentant sinners and does not hold grudges." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### vv. 26–28 — Joab Captures Rabbah's Water Supply

- After the narrative detour, the account returns to the Ammonite war from chapter 11. Joab had fought against Rabbah and captured "the city of waters" (the water supply). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- Ellicott explains: Rabbah was in the narrow valley of the upper Jabbok, on both sides of the stream, with its citadel on the northern cliff. The "royal city" (v. 26) and "city of waters" (v. 27) refer to the city proper (the lower city), while the "city" of vv. 28–29 is the citadel. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- Joab summons David to bring the rest of the troops, "Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me" — giving David the honor of the final victory. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/2-samuel-12.html)

### vv. 29–31 — David Captures Rabbah; The Crown and the Forced Labor

- **The crown** (v. 30): Taken from "their king" (the Hebrew letters also form the name *Milcom*, the chief idol of the Ammonites — some have unnecessarily supposed it was an idol's crown, but most take it as the king's crown). It weighed "a talent of gold." Ellicott: if this is the Hebrew talent, it would be extraordinarily heavy (over 100 lbs for silver, twice that for gold). But various smaller Eastern talents existed (Babylonian, Persian), and one of these lighter talents was likely in use among the Ammonites. Even so, the weight would have been too great for common wearing. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **Forced labor** (v. 31): David "put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and made them work at the brick kilns." Ellicott notes the literal Hebrew ("put them with the saw") doesn't yield good sense; a single letter change brings it into agreement with 1 Chronicles 20:3, "cut them with saws" (cf. Hebrews 11:37). Regarding the "brick-kiln," the Hebrew margin reads "through Malchan" (Molech), leading some to suggest David made them pass through fire. Ellicott says "there is no sufficient reason" to adopt this reading. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **Historical context**: "In the infliction of these cruelties on his enemies David acted in accordance with the customs and the knowledge of his time. Abhorrent as they may be to the spirit of Christianity, David and his contemporaries took them as matters of course." (Ellicott) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)
- **Restoration to military victory**: The chapter ends with David returned to battle and victory — showing that "confession and repentance don't leave us condemned but restored." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives

**Sources specifically consulted but yielding limited tradition-by-tradition contrasts** (search limits prevented full access to gty.org, spurgeon.org, seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu, lcms.org, 1517.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, and netbible.org). The following notes draw on what was available from the approved sites.

### Reformed Perspective
- **Desiring God (John Piper)**: Strong emphasis on the *vertical* nature of sin — sin is fundamentally "assaulting the glory of God." The worst thing David did was "despise the word of God." Also, Piper carefully distinguishes "disciplinary consequences" of forgiven sin from retributive "penalties," arguing the child's death and family turmoil were not punitive but sanctifying. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-consequences-of-forgiven-sin)
- **Monergism** was not directly accessed, but the Reformed understanding (shared broadly) is that David's salvation was secure; the consequences were providential discipline, not condemnation.

### Pentecostal/Charismatic Perspective
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**: Emphasises the *restorative* work of God after repentance — "confession and repentance don't leave us condemned but restored." The commentary stresses practical application about not covering sin, responding immediately to conviction, and the need for specific confession. Also emphasises that extraordinary prayer and fasting are "radical submission" rather than tools to manipulate God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)

### Baptist Perspective
- While gty.org and spurgeon.org were not directly accessible in this search, Spurgeon is quoted multiple times via other sources: he emphasised that David's sin "threw out upon the surface the evil that was always within him" and that God used chastisement as a surgeon's knife to cut out the cancer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-12/)
- The emphasis on the *specificity* of personal confession and the distinction between Saul's false confession and David's genuine one is characteristic of evangelical/Baptist preaching.

### Anglican/Classic Commentary Perspective
- **Ellicott** (Anglican bishop, 19th c.): Careful philological and historical notes — distinguishing the Hebrew verbs for "kill" vs. "murder" in v. 9; explaining the weight of the talent; defending the traditional reading of v. 31 against emendations. Ellicott's pastoral observation that David's "conscience had been stupefied by the delirium of prosperity and power" is particularly insightful. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-12.html)

### Wesleyan/Holiness and Lutheran Perspectives
- Sites seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu, lcms.org, and 1517.org could not be accessed within search limits. No specific Wesleyan or Lutheran distinctions on this chapter could be documented from the available sources.

### Catholic and Orthodox Perspectives
- Sites newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org could not be accessed within search limits. No distinct Catholic or Orthodox readings could be documented. However, it is noted that the Catholic tradition generally understands David's sin as mortal but forgivable through sacramental confession/penance, with temporal consequences remaining — a pattern that aligns broadly with the traditional reading documented above.

### Modern Scholarship
- **NET Bible** notes (accessed partially via preceptaustin.org): A few medieval Hebrew MSS, the LXX, and Syriac Peshitta add "the prophet" after "Nathan" in v. 1. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-12-commentary)
- bibleodyssey.org was not accessed; no further modern critical perspectives available.
